sections.body:
A language model is a program that has been trained to continue text. That is the whole of its job, at the level of the machine. It is not a database of answers. It holds no list of facts about your company, your machine or yesterday's meeting, and when it gives you a fact it did not receive from your text, it produced that fact from a pattern rather than from a record.

What it has is a very large set of numbers, learned from a very large amount of text, that describe which pieces of text tend to follow which other pieces. It has learned that "the pump" is usually followed by a word about pressure or flow. It has learned the shape of a manual, of a complaint, of a code comment, of a safety limit written as a number with a unit. The word "model" means a thing built to stand in for something else: a scale model stands in for a ship, a weather model stands in for the weather. A language model stands in for language itself.

That is also where its limits come from. It has no experience and no self-awareness. It is not conscious, and nothing in it understands what it is saying in the way a person understands it. It has never seen your machine, your customer or your site; everything it says about the world comes from text, and some of that text is old, wrong, or written by someone with an interest in the answer. The practical consequence is simple. You are not talking to a machine that knows things. You are talking to a machine that completes text, and every other point in this article follows from that one difference.
examples: It is not a database of answers; it is a set of tendencies about what comes next.
The model completed the sentence because that continuation was likely, not because it checked a fact.
Nothing in the model knows our machine; everything it said about it came from the text I gave it.
sections.heading: What a language model is, and what it is not

sections.body:
Training happens once, before you ever see the model, and it is expensive. It runs on a very large amount of text, collected from books, articles, websites, code and transcripts. The raw text is first cut into tokens, the chunks a model reads and writes. The model does not read letters.

Then the loop starts, and it is the same loop millions of times over billions of pieces of text. The model is shown a sequence of tokens with the next one hidden. It predicts the hidden token. It compares its prediction with the real one and measures the mistake as a single number. It then adjusts every parameter slightly, in the direction that would have made the mistake smaller. And it moves on to the next sequence.

The parameters are the learned part of the machine: a very large number of weights that hold the tendencies. The name comes from the same root as "measure". Each weight says how much one pattern should raise or lower the chance of another.

The design that made this work came out of the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need", which introduced the transformer, the layer arrangement used by most models today. Its central idea is attention: each token looks at the tokens around it and works out which of them matter for the prediction. The model that answers you is many layers of this, with the parameters inside.

One point is worth holding on to. When you use the model, nothing is being learned. The parameters are fixed. Every answer you get is the same trained model being run forward on your text.
examples: Training is a loop: guess the next token, measure the error, adjust the weights, start again.
Nobody trains the model when I press Enter. The weights were fixed long before.
sections.heading: How a model is trained
steps: Collect a very large amount of text: books, articles, websites, code and transcripts.
Cut the text into tokens, the chunks the model reads.
Show the model a sequence of tokens and hide the next one.
Ask the model to predict the hidden token.
Measure the size of the mistake and adjust every parameter slightly to make it smaller.
Repeat over billions of pieces of text until the mistakes are small enough to be useful.

sections.body:
Your message is cut into tokens. Those tokens are placed in the context window, the space the model can see at once, together with the conversation so far, any document you attached, and the instructions the service was given. The model then does one thing: it predicts the next token. It works out the probability of many possible next tokens, picks one, and writes it down. Then it does the same again with that token added, and again, and again. The answer is built one token at a time, and every new token is chosen from everything that came before it.

This running of a trained model on new text is called inference. It is the opposite of training: the parameters do not change, and nothing is learned from your question. Every answer you receive is one run of inference.

Because each token is picked from a list of likely candidates, the same question can get two different answers. Most services set a control over how much randomness is used in that pick. Low randomness gives you the same answer twice. High randomness gives more variation, and more chance of a wrong turn.

The model also decides when to stop. It produces an end marker, or the service stops it at a length limit, or it stops because the answer called for a tool that has to run first.

And there is no memory between conversations. A new chat begins with nothing, unless the service pastes a summary of the old one back in at the top. That memory lives in a database on the service's side, not in the model, and the model cannot tell the difference between the two.
examples: The answer was built one token at a time, and each token depended on the ones before it.
The weights did not change; the model was only being run forward.
Ask the same question twice and you may get two answers. Both came from the same parameters.
sections.heading: What happens when you press Enter

sections.body:
These seven words are the working vocabulary of the field. They turn up in model documentation, on pricing pages, and in the conversations of people who build these systems.

Four of them describe the machine and the two phases it runs in: **token**, **training data**, **parameters** and **inference**. Two of them describe what you give the model: **prompt** and **context window**. One names the failure that costs the most working time: **hallucination**.

The two phases are worth keeping apart in your head. Training is the long, expensive phase, done by the people who built the model, and it ends before the model reaches you. Inference is every answer you get, one run at a time.

One caution about all seven words. Each one names a mechanism, not a promise. "The model learned" means that it stored a statistical tendency. It does not mean that it knows.
examples: Tokens are the units the model reads; the parameters are the numbers it learned them in.
Training happened once, before I used it. Every answer I get is inference.
If it was not in the context window, the model could not have used it.
sections.heading: The words of the field

terms.example: The word "pump" may be one token, and an unusual part number may be three.
terms.gloss: A piece of text that the model reads and writes as one unit. Usually a word, part of a word, or a common symbol.

terms.example: If the training data was mostly English web pages, the model will answer English best.
terms.gloss: The text a model learns from. Its range and its quality decide what the model is good at and what it never saw.

terms.example: The model has billions of parameters, and not one of them is a sentence you can read.
terms.gloss: The numbers inside a model that hold what it learned. Each one is a weight that raises or lowers the chance of a continuation.

terms.example: Every question you send is one run of inference.
terms.gloss: The phase in which a trained model runs its parameters on a new input to produce an answer.

terms.example: When the context window is full, the first page of the document is no longer in front of the model.
terms.gloss: The amount of text the model can use at one time: your message, the conversation so far, and any attached document.

terms.example: The prompt never said our tolerance, so the answer used the wrong one.
terms.gloss: Everything you send the model: the instruction, the material and the question. It becomes the text the model answers from.

terms.example: The citation was perfect and the paper does not exist. That is a hallucination.
terms.gloss: A fluent, confident answer that is not true. The model produced a likely-looking continuation instead of a fact.

sections.body:
The model was trained to produce likely text, not true text. Truth is not in the objective. It is a good guesser of the next token, and a good guess can be wrong.

A finished answer has two separate qualities: it sounds right, and it is right. The model controls the first one completely. It has no way of knowing the second, because it has no record of what is true, and it never checks a sentence against a source.

Three common causes. The fact was not in the context the model was given, so it filled the gap from the pattern. The fact is rare, and the training text may never have contained it, so the model had nothing to copy. Or the question asked for a source, and the model produced the shape of a citation: a title, an author, a year, all assembled from how citations look rather than from any real document.

When such an answer arrives with the same certainty as a correct one, it is called a hallucination. The name does not mean that the model was confused. It means that the answer has no ground under it. A hallucination can be a made-up number, a made-up quotation, a made-up policy, a made-up file, or a page that does not exist.

There is a second kind of wrongness, and it is quieter. The answer is true, but it is true about something else. The model completed a familiar pattern about another company, another machine or another standard, and the sentence was correct while the subject was wrong.

What follows from all of this is simple. Treat every factual claim as unverified until you have checked it against the source it came from. Fluency is not evidence. It is a property of the writing, not of the claim.
examples: The sentence was fluent and the number was wrong. Fluency is not evidence.
It gave me a reference that looks right; the paper does not exist.
The policy it quoted is a real policy, from another company.
sections.heading: Why a fluent answer can still be wrong

sections.body:
The same mechanism produces both halves of this table, and the difference between them is not luck. Rewriting, summarising, drafting and translating are the tasks a model does well: they are close to the shape of the training text, and the result is judged by how well it reads. Counting, knowing your company and remembering yesterday's conversation are the tasks it does badly: they need information the model does not have, or arithmetic it cannot do without a tool.

Read the bad list as the jobs that stay with you. If you give the model the document, it can summarise the document. If the answer depends on a number from your records, that number is your job. If the job has a state, meaning where it stands, what was decided and what is still open, then you keep that state, because the model keeps nothing.

There is a condition on the good list. Those are the tasks where a good-enough answer is useful and the reader checks the wording rather than the facts. The moment an answer has to carry a number that decides money, time, tolerance or safety, it belongs to the bad list, whatever the answer looks like.
examples: Let it draft the email and you send it. Let it explain the procedure and you check the number at step four.
If the answer needs a number from our records, that check stays with us.
I give it the real text, because it cannot invent the text I forgot to paste.
sections.heading: What a model does well, and what it does badly

rows: Rewriting a text in another tone or length
Arithmetic in its head, without a calculator
Summarising a document you gave it
Counting a long list and getting the total right
Drafting the first version of an email
Explaining a standard procedure step by step
Telling whether the number on the page is the right one

sections.body: Three checks, and the third is the one people skip. **The numbers.** Recalculate anything that decides money, time, tolerance or safety. A model can produce a number with the shape of a correct number and nothing behind it, and the check takes a minute. **The sources.** Open every reference. If the answer cites a paper, a standard or a web page, open it and confirm that it says what the answer claims. A citation with the right shape and the wrong document behind it is the standard failure. **The gaps.** Ask what the model was not given. It does not know your part number, your contract, or yesterday's meeting, so any answer that depends on those is an answer you have to finish yourself. One habit closes all three: ask it to show the steps, then check the steps against a source you trust, and not against the sentence it wrote.
examples: Give me the source for that number and I will check it.
Show me the steps, and mark the part you are not sure about.
Which part of this did you not have? I will supply it.
sections.heading: What to check before you trust the output

sections.body: These sentences explain the behaviour that people find confusing, and they are useful with a colleague, a teacher, or a support line. Use them as they are and change the detail to fit your own situation.
examples: The model did not know that. It completed the text the way the text usually continues.
The answer is fluent and unverified, so I treat it as a draft.
It predicted the next token, and the next token was wrong.
Training is finished. What you are looking at is inference.
There is no memory between chats. The context window is the whole memory.
Give me the real text and I will work from that instead of from what I remember.
Show me the steps, and tell me which part you are not sure about.
sections.heading: Sentences you can reuse

item.summary: A language model does not look up answers. It learns patterns from a large amount of text, and at run time it predicts the next token, one token at a time. After reading this you can explain how a model is trained, what the context window holds, why a fluent answer can be wrong, and what to check before you trust an output at work.
item.title: How AI Actually Works: Training, Prediction and Its Limits
